analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for everyone and pays for it with new taxes on income above $250,000 and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2025 with 10 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would increase every Social Security check by changing the benefit formula, switch cost-of-living adjustments to an index that tracks what seniors actually buy, set a new minimum benefit near the poverty line for long-time low earners, and let children of deceased or disabled workers receive benefits through age 22 as full-time students. To pay for it and extend Social Security's solvency, it would apply the payroll tax to wages above $250,000 and raise the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries — especially low-earning retirees, widows, and disabled workers — would get larger checks, a higher cost-of-living adjustment tied to seniors' actual spending, and a new minimum benefit near the poverty line for people who worked 11+ years. Children of deceased or disabled workers could keep collecting benefits as full-time students up to age 22. The tax changes apply to people earning above $250,000 and to investment income, so the financing falls on high earners and investors rather than on a typical worker's paycheck.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first bend point from 90% to 95% and boosts it by an additional 18%, which increases every beneficiary's monthly check — the largest gains in dollar terms go to those with the lowest earnings histories.

Creates a new minimum benefit scaled to the federal poverty line, reaching 125% of that amount for workers with 30 or more years of work, so a full-career low earner can no longer retire below poverty.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the CPI for Elderly Consumers, an index that tracks what people over 62 actually buy (more health care, less electronics), typically producing slightly larger annual increases.
Lets children of deceased or disabled workers keep receiving benefits as full-time students until age 22, instead of losing them at 18-19, easing the cost of college for surviving families.
Applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages above $250,000 and raises the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 16.2%, directing the revenue into the trust fund to extend its solvency.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with wage, self-employment, or business income above $250,000, who would face Social Security payroll taxes on income above that level for the first time; and investors, whose net investment income tax would rise from 3.8% to 16.2%. Businesses employing high earners would remit part of the new payroll tax.

drawbacks.text: Raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 16.2% is a steep tax on investment returns; critics argue it would discourage investment and could push some high earners to convert income into forms the tax does not reach.

Extending payroll taxes above $250,000 breaks the historical link between what a worker pays in and what they receive — high earners would pay more taxes without receiving proportionally higher benefits, which opponents frame as turning Social Security partway into a welfare program.
The bill raises benefits at the same time it taxes more, so if the new revenue falls short of projections, the long-term financing fix is less certain than its sponsors suggest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: higher checks for every beneficiary, a much higher floor for the poorest retirees, better inflation protection, and college-age children of disabled or deceased workers supported through age 22 — all financed by taxes that fall almost entirely on high earners and investors, not on a typical working household. The main honest concerns are the design and the politics: the CPI-E and the big bend-point change make the growth in benefits permanent and compounding, so if the new taxes underperform the projections, the trust fund's solvency is less certain than the bill's framing suggests; the 16.2% investment tax is far above any existing U.S. rate and its behavioral and revenue effects are untested; and the payroll-tax gap over $250,000 changes the historical link between what top earners pay in and what they eventually receive. None of these concerns rises to the level of the benefits at stake for low-income seniors, who today can retire into poverty on a Social Security check alone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on February 27, 2025, and no committee action, hearing, or vote has followed.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the Social Security Expansion Act in the Senate on February 27, 2025.
Ten Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill alongside Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Finance Committee.
As of the end of the available record, the Finance Committee has taken no action on the bill — no hearings, no markup, no vote — so it has never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households are better off so far: the payroll tax cap above $250,000 and the higher investment income tax have not been enacted, and current law's benefit formula remains unchanged.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the cosponsors.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Warren, Merkley, Welch, Padilla, Smith, Van Hollen, Markey, Booker, Gillibrand, Whitehouse)

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for any Senate action; no Republican supported it, and with 55 of 100 seats the majority can keep it from ever reaching the floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has taken no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor is a Democrat or an independent aligned with Democrats — 10 of 45 Senate Democrats — and no Senate Republican supports the bill, so the bill's fate depends entirely on whether the Democratic minority can force it onto the agenda, which it cannot by itself.

industries.industry: High earners and investors (households with income above $250,000)
industries.note: The bill pays for its benefit increases with a new payroll tax above $250,000 and a quadrupling-plus of the net investment income tax to 16.2%, falling almost entirely on the top few percent of households. Their Social Security benefit increase is far smaller than their added tax.

industries.industry: High-income business owners and the self-employed
industries.note: The bill extends the net investment income tax to active business income and applies the self-employment tax above $250,000, closing routes that let business owners shield earnings from these taxes.

industries.industry: Wealthy taxpayers' tax-planning and financial services
industries.note: Closing the 'active trade or business' loophole in the investment income tax and applying payroll tax above $250,000 reduces demand for structures that reclassify labor income as investment or business income.
Extending child benefits to age 22 for full-time students acts as a de facto public income supplement for students from families that lost a working parent, reducing reliance on loans.

analysis.trajectory: Bills of this kind referred to the Finance Committee without bipartisan cosponsors almost never get a hearing, markup, or floor vote in this Congress. With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and none sponsoring the bill, the realistic path is that it sits in committee and dies at the end of the 119th Congress.
